author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Academic register: nominalisation, hedging and impersonal style
summary: Academic English is not just longer words. It packages ideas into noun phrases, qualifies claims carefully, keeps the writer in the background and avoids informal features. This lesson brings together the grammar behind that style.

blocks.text: Register is the choice of language to suit reader, purpose and medium. Academic register is **precise, objective, cautious and dense**. Four grammatical tools create it: nominalisation, hedging, impersonal structures and formal vocabulary and linking.
Turning verbs and adjectives into nouns lets you treat processes as things and pack more information into a sentence.

head: Verbal style
Nominal style
rows: Prices increased quickly, which worried consumers.
**The rapid increase in prices** worried consumers.
We analysed the data and found that…
Because people are using cars less, …

blocks.text: Too much nominalisation becomes unreadable. Keep a clear subject and an active verb where possible.

head: Tool
Examples
rows: *appear to, seem to, tend to, suggest, indicate*
*it is likely/possible that; there is evidence that*
*some, many, in most cases, to some extent*

items.en: Social media **causes** depression.
Heavy social-media use **appears to be associated with** higher rates of depression **in some groups**.

items: Passive: *The samples **were tested**.*
Anticipatory *it*: ***It is widely accepted that** … **It could be argued that** …*
*There* + be: ***There is** little evidence to support this view.*
Abstract subjects: ***This study** examines… **The data** suggest…*

blocks.text: *I* and *we* are increasingly accepted in many disciplines, but IELTS-style essays usually avoid *I think*: prefer *In my view* once, or impersonal forms.

head: Informal
Academic
rows: a great deal of, numerous, a large number of

items.en: ~~Nowadays, there are a lot of people who think that technology is very bad for kids.~~
items.note: *Many people now argue that technology may harm children's development.*

items.en: ~~Scientists have proved that coffee is healthy.~~
items.note: Overclaiming: *Research suggests that moderate coffee consumption may have health benefits.*

items.en: ~~The government should solve this problem fast.~~
items.note: Vague: *Governments could address the problem by…*

items: **Boosters** for well-supported claims: *clearly, undoubtedly, demonstrate, it is evident that*. Balance boosters and hedges.
**Evaluative stance markers**: *Surprisingly, Notably, Importantly*.
**Cohesion through reference**: *this trend, such policies, these findings* (a summary noun after *this/these*).

blocks.text: Aim for a formal-neutral tone: clear topic sentences, hedged claims, varied linking, no contractions or slang. Over-formality (*Henceforth, it is incumbent upon*) is as unnatural as informality. Clarity always comes first.

items: Nominalise to condense, but keep sentences readable.
Hedge claims to match the strength of your evidence.
Use impersonal structures and abstract subjects.
Replace informal words, contractions and phrasal verbs.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Adjectives, adverbs and intensifiers: gradability, position and order
summary: Choosing the right intensifier depends on whether an adjective is gradable. Adverb position changes focus and meaning, and adjective order follows a logic native speakers feel but rarely explain.

blocks.text: Adjectives and adverbs carry much of the precision in advanced English: *a **marginally** better result*, *a **deeply** flawed argument*, *an **utterly** convincing case*. Three systems decide whether these combinations sound natural: **gradability** (which intensifiers an adjective accepts), **position** (where an adverb sits and what it modifies) and **order** (how several adjectives line up before a noun).

sections.title: How it works: gradable and non-gradable adjectives

blocks.text: **Gradable** adjectives describe qualities that exist in degrees: *cold, interesting, important*. You can have more or less of them, so they combine with **grading adverbs**: *very, extremely, fairly, rather, slightly, a bit*. **Non-gradable** adjectives describe either an **extreme** (*freezing, fascinating, essential*) or an **absolute/classifying** category (*unique, impossible, dead, nuclear, annual*). They already contain the idea of "maximum" or "either-or", so *very* sounds illogical: *~~very freezing~~, ~~very unique~~*. Instead they take **non-grading adverbs**: *absolutely, completely, totally, utterly* (extremes) or *almost, nearly, virtually, practically* (absolutes).
*Really* and *pretty* work with both types in informal English; *quite* changes meaning: *quite good* = fairly good (gradable), *quite brilliant* = completely brilliant (non-gradable).

head: Adjective type
Typical adverbs
Examples
rows: very, extremely, highly, fairly, rather, slightly, somewhat, a little

blocks.text: Strong adverb–adjective collocations

Advanced English relies on fixed pairings rather than *very*: *bitterly disappointed, deeply concerned, highly controversial, painfully slow, strikingly similar, fundamentally different, widely available, readily accessible, acutely aware, sorely missed, vastly superior, heavily dependent.*
Adverb positions

items: **front**: connecting and comment adverbs: *Fortunately, the data were saved.*
**mid** (before the main verb, after be/first auxiliary): frequency, focus, certainty: *She has **probably** left. They **rarely** reply.*
**end**: manner, place, time: *He spoke **quietly** in the hall **yesterday**.*

blocks.text: Adjective order before a noun

opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose + noun: *a **beautiful old Italian marble** fountain*, *a **small round wooden** table*. Usually no more than three adjectives appear together in natural English.
1. Precision instead of emphasis
*very important* is vague; *critically important*, *of central importance* or *paramount* are precise. In formal writing, prefer a stronger adjective or a collocating adverb to stacking *very*.
2. Downtoning and hedging
*somewhat, slightly, relatively, fairly, comparatively* soften claims: *The effect was **relatively** small.* Academic writing uses these to avoid overstatement.
3. Focus through position
Moving an adverb changes what it modifies: *She **only** teaches on Fridays* (and nothing else on Fridays? or only on Fridays?) is ambiguous in writing; *She teaches **only** on Fridays* is precise.
4. Comment versus manner

*She answered the question **honestly**.* (manner: how she answered) / ***Honestly**, she answered the question.* (comment: the speaker's frankness). Front position turns many manner adverbs into comment adverbs: *clearly, frankly, naturally, seriously.*

items.en: The proposal is **highly controversial** and **deeply unpopular** with staff.
It is **virtually impossible** to verify the claim.
The two cases are **strikingly similar** in their outcomes.
I was **absolutely furious**, not just annoyed.
The results are **broadly consistent** with earlier studies.
**Clearly**, the policy has failed. / He didn't explain it **clearly**.
a **charming little eighteenth-century stone** cottage

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *hard* = with effort (*work hard*); *hardly* = almost not (*I hardly know her*)
*arrive late* vs *recently* (*I haven't slept well lately*)
literal height vs degree: *aim high* / *highly recommended*
without payment vs without restriction: *travel free* / *speak freely*
superlative vs mainly: *the most useful* / *mostly useful*
*fairly* is neutral or positive; *rather* often suggests surprise or criticism: *rather expensive*

blocks.text: Informal: *really, so, super, pretty, totally*. Neutral: *very, quite, extremely*. Formal/academic: *highly, considerably, substantially, markedly, relatively, comparatively, somewhat*.

In academic writing, intensifiers are used sparingly; overuse of *extremely* or *absolutely* sounds emotional. Precision comes from evidence and from exact collocations: *a **statistically significant** difference*, *a **markedly** higher rate*.

items.en: ~~The view was very breathtaking.~~
~~This is a very unique opportunity.~~
items.note: This is a unique opportunity. / This is a truly unique opportunity.

items.en: ~~She speaks very well English.~~
~~I hardly worked to finish the project.~~
items.note: I worked hard to finish the project.

items.en: ~~a wooden old big table~~
~~The results were highly disappointed.~~

blocks.text: Intensifying with structure rather than adverbs

*Not only is the method slow, it is **far from** reliable.* *Nothing could be **further from** the truth.* *The difference is **by no means** trivial.* Litotes and negated adverbs give controlled emphasis in formal prose.
Adjective complementation

Many adjectives require specific patterns: *aware **of***, *conducive **to***, *consistent **with***, *reluctant **to do***, *it is imperative **that** ...*. Getting the complement right matters as much as the intensifier.
Post-positive adjectives

Some adjectives follow the noun: *the people **involved**, the members **present**, the issues **concerned**, something **new**, the best solution **available**.* The position can change meaning: *the **concerned** parent* (worried) vs *the parent **concerned*** (the one in question).

items: Gradable adjectives take *very, extremely, fairly*; extreme and absolute adjectives take *absolutely, completely, virtually*.
Learn adverb–adjective collocations (*deeply concerned, highly unlikely*) instead of *very*.
Adverb position affects focus and meaning; front position often gives a comment adverb.
Adjective order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.
Formal writing prefers precise adverbs (*markedly, considerably, relatively*) and avoids emotional intensifiers.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Anticipatory it and there: extraposition and existential sentences
summary: English dislikes long subjects at the front of a sentence. Anticipatory "it" and existential "there" move heavy information to the end, where it is easier to process and naturally stressed.

blocks.text: *To find a flat in central Vienna is difficult* is grammatical but sounds heavy. Native speakers say ***It** is difficult to find a flat in central Vienna.* The empty subject *it* "anticipates" the real subject, which moves to the end. Similarly, ***There** are three reasons for this* introduces new information more naturally than *Three reasons for this are*. Mastering these two dummy subjects is one of the clearest differences between intermediate and advanced writing.

sections.title: How it works: end-weight and end-focus

blocks.text: Two principles of English information structure explain both constructions:

items: **End-weight**: long, complex constituents go at the end of the clause, where the listener has already processed the verb.
**End-focus**: new and important information goes at the end, where sentence stress naturally falls.

blocks.text: A that-clause, wh-clause or to-infinitive subject is usually both long and new, so English moves it to the end and fills the subject position with **it** (*extraposition*). When we introduce something new into the discourse, English uses **there + be** (*existential there*), placing the new noun phrase after the verb.
*It* refers forward to a clause; *there* introduces the existence or presence of something. *~~There is important to check~~* is wrong; *It is important to check* is right.
Anticipatory it

head: Pattern
Example
rows: *It is **a pity** that you missed it. It was **a mistake** to wait.*
*It **surprised** me that she agreed. It **took** years to finish.*
*It **is believed** that the fire started accidentally.*
*I **find it** hard to concentrate. We **consider it** essential that ...*

blocks.text: Existential there

head: Pattern
Example
rows: *There were students **waiting** outside. There were two people **injured**.*
there + passive reporting verb + to be
*There **are said to be** over a thousand species.*

blocks.text: The verb after *there* agrees with the following noun: *There **is** a reason / There **are** two reasons.* In informal speech *there's* is often used with plurals (*there's lots of people*), but not in writing.
1. Evaluating with adjectives
*It is **crucial / doubtful / worth noting / widely accepted** that ...* lets the writer evaluate an idea before stating it. This is central to academic stance.
2. Distancing and hedging with reporting verbs
*It **is often argued** that ..., It **has been suggested** that ..., It **would seem** that ...* present claims without naming a source or committing fully.
3. Introducing topics and listing
*There are several factors to consider. There is little evidence that ... There is no doubt that ...*
4. Time and distance
*It's two years since we met. It takes three hours to get there. It's a long way to the coast.*
5. Object it

After *find, make, consider, think, believe* the infinitive or that-clause cannot directly follow the verb: *I find **it** difficult to explain* (~~I find difficult to explain~~). *The new rules make **it** easier to apply.*

items.en: It is worth noting that the sample was drawn from urban areas only.
items.note: evaluation before the point, a useful limitation statement

items.en: It has been estimated that a third of food is wasted.
There is growing concern about the use of facial recognition.
There appears to be no simple solution.
The software makes it possible to track changes in real time.
It was not until the 1960s that the theory was accepted.
There remain several unanswered questions.

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *It is said that X* vs *X is said to*
two impersonal passives: *It is said that the castle is haunted* / *The castle is said to be haunted*. The second makes the castle the topic.
the existential version: *There is said to be gold in the hills.*
*It is surprising **that** she left* (extraposition: *it* = that she left) vs *It was **Maria** **who** left* (cleft: focuses on Maria; remove *it was ... who* and a full sentence remains).
*It is a problem* (the situation already mentioned is a problem) vs *There is a problem* (a problem exists; new information).
*It took me an hour to finish* (time required) vs *I needed an hour to finish*. Both correct; *it takes* is more idiomatic for time.

blocks.text: Academic writing relies heavily on anticipatory *it* to evaluate and hedge (*It is likely / possible / clear / important that*). Overuse, however, produces a string of empty openings. Vary with personal or noun subjects: *These results suggest ...*, *A plausible explanation is ...*.
In speech, *there's* + plural and the object-*it* pattern are frequent; existential *there* with verbs other than *be* (*there exists, there arose*) is formal or literary.

items.en: ~~Is important to analyse the results.~~
items.note: It is important to analyse the results.

items.en: ~~There is important to remember the context.~~
items.note: It is important to remember the context.

items.en: ~~I find difficult to concentrate in the library.~~
items.note: I find it difficult to concentrate in the library.

items.en: ~~It exists a strong link between diet and health.~~
items.note: There is a strong link between diet and health.

items.en: ~~There is many reasons for this.~~
items.note: There are many reasons for this.

items.en: ~~It is said the fire to have started at night.~~
items.note: The fire is said to have started at night. / It is said that the fire started at night.

blocks.text: Extraposition from noun phrases
Long post-modifiers can also move to the end: *A rumour spread **that the CEO had resigned**.* (instead of *A rumour that the CEO had resigned spread*). The result is lighter and clearer.
Combining hedges
*It would **appear** that there **may** be some grounds for concern.* Multiple hedges signal caution but can make a claim vanish; use them in proportion to the strength of the evidence.
There + negative quantifiers for strong claims
*There is **no** evidence that ..., There is **little** reason to believe ..., There is **every** reason to expect ...* give a confident, compact verdict.

items: Move long subject clauses to the end with anticipatory *it*: *It is clear that ...*.
Use object *it* after *find, make, consider*: *I find it hard to ...*.
Use *there + be* to introduce new things; the verb agrees with the following noun.
Impersonal passives: *It is said that X* / *X is said to* / *There is said to be*.
Do not confuse extraposition with the *it*-cleft.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Articles, countability, quantifiers and complex noun phrases
summary: Articles are one of the hardest areas for speakers of languages without them. This lesson covers a, the and no article, countability, quantifiers, and how advanced writers pack information into noun phrases.

blocks.text: A noun phrase is a noun plus everything that describes or limits it: *the **three** **rather old** **wooden** chairs **in the hall***. Determiners (*a, the, some, every, this*) tell the listener whether the thing is known, how much or how many.

sections.title: a/an, the and no article: the core rules

head: Use
When
Example
rows: one of many, first mention, jobs, classifying
already known or unique; second mention; superlatives
***The** fox ran away. **The** sun. **The** best day.*
plural or uncountable nouns used in general

items.en: I love **music**.
I love **the music** in this film.
~~The life is beautiful.~~

items: **Generic *the*** for a whole class (formal, technical): ***The** tiger is endangered. **The** computer changed work.*
Institutions with no article when used for their purpose: *go to **school**, be in **hospital**, go to **prison**, at **university*** (but *visit **the** hospital*).

Places: no article for most countries, cities, lakes, single mountains; *the* for rivers, seas, mountain ranges, plural or "state/kingdom/republic" names: ***the** Volga, **the** Alps, **the** Netherlands, **the** UK*.
Meals, sports, languages, academic subjects: no article (*have **lunch**, play **chess**, study **law***).

blocks.text: Uncountable nouns have no plural and take singular verbs: *advice, information, research, evidence, equipment, furniture, news, progress, knowledge, accommodation (BrE), luggage, homework, traffic*.

items.en: ~~She gave me many advices.~~
items.note: *She gave me a lot of advice / several pieces of advice.*

items.en: The news **is** good.

blocks.text: Some nouns are countable and uncountable with different meanings: *a paper* (newspaper/essay) vs *paper*; *an experience* (event) vs *experience* (skill); *a light* vs *light*.

head: With countable plural
With uncountable
With both
rows: many, (a) few, several, a number of
much, (a) little, a great deal of, an amount of
some, any, a lot of, plenty of, most, all, no

items.en: **Few** people came.
**A few** people came.
**Each / Every** student has a laptop.
**Neither** answer is correct. **None of** the answers is/are correct.

blocks.text: Advanced writing packs information into noun phrases instead of using several clauses:

items.en: Prices rose rapidly, and this worried consumers. → ***The rapid rise in prices** worried consumers.*

blocks.text: Tools: noun modifiers (*a **government** report*), compound adjectives (*a **two-hour** delay*, *a **well-known** author*), prepositional phrases (*the impact **of social media on teenagers***), and post-modifying clauses (*a decision **likely to anger voters***).
Compound adjectives with numbers have no plural: *a **five-year** plan*, not ~~five-years plan~~.

items.en: ~~I am student.~~
items.note: Jobs and roles need *a/an*: *I am a student.*

items.en: ~~The most of people agree.~~
items.note: *Most people agree.* / *Most of the people I asked agree.*

items.en: ~~We need more informations.~~
~~He is in the hospital since Monday.~~
items.note: BrE: *He has been in hospital since Monday.*

blocks.text: Academic writing relies on long noun phrases and generic reference: *The introduction of tuition fees has led to a decline in applications from low-income students.* Countable/uncountable precision matters: *a growing body of **research**, a number of **studies**, an amount of **evidence**.*

items: a/an = one of many or first mention; the = known/unique; zero = general plural/uncountable.
Learn the common uncountable nouns; use *a piece of / an item of* to count them.
few (negative) vs a few (positive); much/little with uncountable.
Advanced writing compresses clauses into noun phrases.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Cohesion and reference: this, such, the former, summary nouns and given-new order
summary: A text holds together through reference: pronouns, determiners and summary nouns that point back to ideas. Clear reference, plus a given-before-new order, is what makes advanced writing easy to follow.

blocks.text: Linking words (*however, therefore*) are only one source of cohesion. Most of the connection between sentences comes from **reference**: *This shift, such policies, the former, these findings, the latter approach*. Readers constantly ask "what does *this* refer to?". If the answer is unclear, the argument breaks down even when each sentence is grammatical.

sections.title: How it works: pointing back and the given-new contract

blocks.text: Reference words create chains across sentences:

items: **Personal reference**: *it, they, them, its* — refer to a specific noun.
**Demonstrative reference**: *this, that, these, those* — refer to nouns **or** to whole ideas.
**Comparative reference**: *such, similar, other, the same, the former / the latter*.
**Lexical reference**: a new noun that summarises the previous idea: *This **decline** ..., The **proposal** ..., These **findings** ...*

blocks.text: English prose also follows a **given-new contract**: a sentence usually starts with information the reader already has (given) and ends with new information. Reference words typically sit at the **start** of the sentence, linking back, while the new point comes at the end.
In formal writing, follow *this/these* with a noun when the reference could be unclear: *This **trend** ...* rather than *This ...* alone.

head: Device
Pattern
Example
rows: refer to the first / second of two
*We tested X and Y; **the latter** proved more reliable.*
*The old model is cheaper than **the new one**.*
substitute for a verb phrase or clause
*Few firms **did so**. I hope **so**. I'm afraid **not**.*

blocks.text: Common summary nouns

*approach, argument, assumption, claim, concern, development, difficulty, distinction, factor, finding, issue, method, pattern, phenomenon, process, shift, situation, tendency, trend, view*. Choosing a precise summary noun also **evaluates** the previous content: *this **claim*** (doubtful), *this **finding*** (established), *this **problem*** (negative).
1. Avoiding repetition without losing clarity
*The government introduced a sugar tax in 2018. The tax / This levy / Such a measure ...* Each choice keeps the topic but varies the wording.
2. Evaluating while referring
*Some argue that homework is unnecessary. This **view** ignores ... / This **claim** is weakly supported ...* The noun lets you judge the idea as you return to it.
3. Building paragraphs

Topic sentence → development sentences beginning with given information → conclusion: *Remote work has grown rapidly. **This growth** has been uneven, however. **The largest increases** occurred in ...*
4. Managing two items
*the former / the latter* for exactly two items; for more than two use *the first, the second, the last*. *Respectively* pairs two lists.

items.en: Unemployment fell while wages stagnated. **This combination** puzzled economists.
items.note: summary noun for two linked facts

items.en: Two models were tested: a linear one and a neural network. **The latter** performed better.
Several councils have banned cars from school streets. **Such schemes** reduce pollution at peak times.
The survey had a low response rate. **This limitation** should be borne in mind.
items.note: summary noun evaluates the fact as a weakness

items.en: Men and women reported 6.1 and 7.4 hours of sleep, **respectively**.
Many students intend to study abroad, but few **do so**.
**These findings** suggest that ...

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *this* = close, current, the writer's focus; *that* = more distant or the other person's point: *That is not what I said.* In academic writing *this* is far more frequent for back-reference.

*it* refers to a specific noun; *this* can refer to a whole preceding idea: *She resigned. **This** surprised everyone* (the fact of resigning). *It surprised everyone* is possible but less clearly about the whole event.
*latter* = second of two only; for three or more, *the last*.
identical vs alike: *the same results* / *similar results*.

blocks.text: Academic and professional writing relies on summary nouns and *such*; conversation relies on *it, that, this thing, stuff like that*. *The former/the latter* and *respectively* are formal and best used in writing.
Overusing bare *this* (*This shows that this is why this happens*) is a common weakness. One clear summary noun is worth several vague pronouns.

items.en: ~~The company cut costs and closed two factories. This caused protests. (ambiguous: which?)~~
items.note: The closure of the factories caused protests.

items.en: ~~There are three options; the latter is the cheapest.~~
items.note: There are three options; the last is the cheapest.

items.en: ~~Such a policies are unpopular.~~
items.note: Such policies are unpopular. / Such a policy is unpopular.

items.en: ~~Group A and Group B improved by 5% and 9% respectively each.~~
items.note: Groups A and B improved by 5% and 9%, respectively.

items.en: ~~Pollution is a serious problem. These problem affects cities.~~
~~The results were good and it showed that the method works.~~
items.note: The results were good, which showed that ... / These results show that ...

blocks.text: Encapsulation and evaluation

Summary nouns can encapsulate a whole paragraph and steer the reader's view: *This **oversimplification** ...*, *This **paradox** ...*, *This **apparent contradiction** ...*. Choosing between *claim, argument, finding, assumption* is a stance decision.
Thematic progression

Advanced writers alternate patterns: (1) the same theme continues (*Remote work ... It ... It ...*); (2) the new information of one sentence becomes the theme of the next (*... caused a shortage. **This shortage** ...*). Pattern (2) creates forward momentum in argument.
Cataphoric reference
Reference can point forward: ***This** is the key point: costs are rising faster than revenue.* *The following* and colons create anticipation in presentations and reports.

items: Reference links sentences: *it, this, such, the former/latter, one, do so*.
Use *this/these* + a summary noun when reference could be unclear.
Summary nouns (*trend, claim, finding*) both refer and evaluate.
Start sentences with given information; end with new information.
*The latter* only for two items; *respectively* matches two lists in order.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Comparison, degree and modification
summary: Precise comparison is central to academic writing and data description. This lesson covers comparatives and superlatives, modifiers of degree, as…as structures and advanced ways of comparing.

blocks.text: Comparison expresses differences or similarities in degree. Advanced users go beyond *bigger than* to say **how much** bigger and to compare with precision.

head: Adjective
Comparative
Superlative
rows: the best, the worst, the furthest

blocks.text: Some two-syllable adjectives take both forms: *simpler / more simple*, *narrower*, *quieter*.

head: Big difference
Small difference
With superlatives
rows: much, far, a lot, considerably, significantly
slightly, a little, a bit, marginally
by far, easily, quite, the second/third …

items.en: Rents are **considerably higher** in the capital.
This is **by far the best** option.
~~It is very cheaper.~~

items: **as … as / not as (so) … as**: *It's **not as easy as** it looks.*
**twice / three times as … as**: *Housing costs **twice as much as** it did.*
**the + comparative, the + comparative**: ***The more** you practise, **the easier** it gets.*
**comparative + and + comparative**: *It's getting **harder and harder**.*
**the same as / similar to / different from**: *My view is **similar to** yours.*

items.en: There's **nowhere near as** much traffic as there used to be.
The results were **nothing like as** clear as we hoped.
Unemployment is **not nearly as** high as predicted.
Prices are **on a par with** those in Paris.
**Compared with / In comparison with** 2010, crime has fallen.
**Whereas / While** the north is industrial, the south relies on tourism.
Exports rose **by** 5%, **from** 20 **to** 21 billion.
further / farther
items.note: both for distance; only *further* = additional (*further information*)

items.en: elder / older
items.note: *elder* only before nouns for family members (*my elder brother*); not with *than*

items.en: less / fewer
~~She is more taller than me.~~
~~It's the most good restaurant.~~
~~My bag is the same like yours.~~

blocks.text: Data descriptions combine comparatives with precise modifiers: *Spending rose marginally, whereas investment fell sharply.* Avoid vague intensifiers (*very, really*) in favour of *substantially, slightly, approximately, roughly twice as*.

items: Use *much/far/considerably* or *slightly/marginally* to show the size of a difference.
*as … as*, *twice as … as*, *the more…the more*.
C1: *nowhere near as, on a par with, compared with, whereas*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Conditionals, wishes and the unreal past
summary: Conditionals link a condition to a result. Advanced use includes mixed conditionals, alternatives to if, implied conditions and the unreal past after wish, if only, it's time and would rather.

blocks.text: A conditional sentence has a **condition clause** (often with *if*) and a **result clause**. The tenses show whether the situation is real or imagined, and its time.

head: Type
Condition
Result
Meaning
rows: general truths: *If you heat ice, it melts.*
real future: *If it rains, we'll stay in.*
unreal present/future: *If I had time, I'd help.*
unreal past: *If we'd left earlier, we'd have caught it.*

blocks.text: *If I were* is preferred to *If I was* in formal English: *If I were you, I'd apologise.*
Mix times when a past condition has a present result, or a present state explains a past result:

items.en: If I **had taken** the job, I **would be living** in Berlin now.
If she **weren't** so shy, she **would have spoken** up at the meeting.

head: Conjunction
Meaning
Example
rows: provided / providing (that), as long as, on condition that
*You can borrow it **as long as** you return it.*
***Supposing** you lost your job, what would you do?*
***But for** your help, I would have failed.*

sections.title: The unreal past: wish, if only, it's time, would rather

blocks.text: You cannot use *wish + would* about yourself: ~~I wish I would be taller~~ → *I wish I were taller*.

items.en: If I see him, I'll tell him.
If I saw him, I'd tell him.
Take a coat **in case** it gets cold.
items.note: precaution, whether or not it gets cold

items.en: Take a coat **if** it gets cold.
**Should** you need help, call me.
~~If I would have known, I would have come.~~
items.note: No *would* in the if-clause: *If I had known…*

items.en: ~~Unless you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.~~
~~I wish I can speak Japanese.~~

items: **Inverted conditionals** (formal): *Had I known* = If I had known; *Were it not for* = If it were not for; *Should you require* = If you require.
**Implied conditions** without a condition clause: *I'd have called, but my battery died.* / *A smaller company would never have survived.*
**if + will** for willingness or result: *If you'll follow me, I'll show you your room.*
**if + should** for unlikely events: *If anything should go wrong, call this number.*

blocks.text: Academic writers use conditionals to state assumptions and limitations: *If these trends continue, demand will exceed supply by 2040.* *Were the sample larger, the results might differ.* Inversion and *provided that* sound formal; *as long as* and *what if* are neutral or informal.

items: Zero/first = real; second/third = unreal present/past; mix them for cross-time meaning.
*unless* = except if; *in case* = precaution; *provided/as long as* = only if.
Unreal past after *wish, if only, it's time, would rather*.
Formal inversion: *Had I…, Were it…, Should you…*

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Dependent prepositions after verbs, adjectives and nouns
summary: Many verbs, adjectives and nouns are followed by a fixed preposition. There is often no logical rule, so the best strategy is to learn them as chunks and notice patterns by meaning.

blocks.text: A **dependent preposition** is the preposition that a particular word "chooses". You learn *depend **on***, *interested **in***, *a reason **for*** as single units.

items.en: It **depends on** the weather.
She's **interested in** urban design.
What's the **reason for** the delay?

blocks.text: After a preposition, use a **noun**, a **pronoun** or an **-ing** form: *I'm thinking **of moving**.* (~~of move~~, ~~of to move~~)

blocks.title: Questions and relative clauses: the preposition moves to the end

items.en: What are you **worried about**?
the project **(that) I'm responsible for**
the project **for which** I am responsible

blocks.text: Verbs

head: Preposition
Verbs
rows: depend, rely, insist, concentrate, comment, focus, spend (money)
believe, specialise, succeed, invest, participate, result (= cause)
apologise, apply, pay, search, wait, blame sb, thank sb
accuse sb, approve, consist, remind sb, warn sb, dream (= imagine)
benefit, recover, suffer, prevent sb, protect sb, differ
agree, cope, deal, provide sb, cooperate, charge sb
belong, object, react, refer, respond, adapt, contribute

blocks.text: Adjectives

head: Preposition
Adjectives
rows: afraid, aware, capable, fond, jealous, proud, tired, typical
anxious, excited, upset, worried, sure, enthusiastic
good, bad, brilliant, hopeless, surprised, amazed
angry, bored, familiar, satisfied, pleased, obsessed
similar, equal, addicted, kind, polite, opposed
famous, responsible, suitable, eligible, grateful (for sth)

blocks.text: Nouns

head: Preposition
Nouns
rows: increase, rise, fall, decrease, change, interest, difference
demand, need, reason, respect, responsibility, cure
solution, answer, access, approach, attitude, threat, alternative
effect, impact, influence, ban, tax, emphasis

head: Phrase
Meaning
rows: **angry with** a person / **angry about** a situation
**agree with** a person or opinion / **agree to** a proposal / **agree on** a decision
accept a view / accept a plan / reach a joint decision
*What do you think **of** it?* / *I'm thinking **about** it.*
*Stress can result **in** illness.* / *Illness can result **from** stress.*
**responsible for** a task / **responsible to** a person

items.en: ~~It depends of the price.~~
~~She's married with a doctor.~~
~~We discussed about the plan.~~
items.note: *discuss* takes a direct object: *discussed the plan* (but *a discussion **about***)

items.en: ~~I'm looking forward to see you.~~
items.note: *to* is a preposition here: *looking forward to **seeing***

items.en: ~~The impact to society is significant.~~
~~He entered into the room.~~
items.note: *enter* takes a direct object: *entered the room* (*enter into* = begin an agreement)

items.en: The findings **shed light on** the causes of poverty.
The study **draws on** data from twelve countries.
Access **to** education is a key **determinant of** income.
**In contrast to** earlier research, this survey found no link **between** age and satisfaction.

blocks.text: Formal writing often places the preposition before *which/whom*: *the conditions **under which** they work*, *the colleague **to whom** I reported*.
Learn the word **with** its preposition. After any preposition, use a noun or **-ing**.

items: *depend on, consist of, insist on, succeed in, apologise for*
*good at, interested in, aware of, similar to, responsible for*
*increase in, impact on, solution to, reason for, lack of*

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Ellipsis and substitution: leaving words out and replacing them
summary: Fluent speakers avoid repeating words. They replace them with so, not, one, do or that, or simply leave them out. These tools make speech and writing concise and cohesive.

blocks.text: **Substitution** replaces a word or phrase with a shorter form; **ellipsis** leaves it out completely because the listener can recover it from context.

items.en: "Is it going to rain?" "I hope **not**."
I wanted a large coffee but they only had small **ones**.
She said she'd help, and she **did**.
"Coming tonight?" "Can't, sorry."
items.note: Ellipsis in informal speech: *Are you* and *I* are left out.

blocks.text: Only leave out or replace what the listener can recover **unambiguously** from the text or situation.

head: Replaces
Substitute
Example
rows: This chair is broken — take the other **one**.
a clause after think, hope, expect, suppose, be afraid, guess
He promised to call, and he **did**. / If you want to leave, **do so** now.
a verb phrase after modals and auxiliaries
I didn't want to go, but I had **to**.

blocks.text: Negative forms with so/not

items: After **and, but, or** you can leave out a repeated subject or auxiliary: *She opened the letter **and** (she) read it twice.*
In comparisons: *He earns more than I do / than me.*
After **wh-** words: *Someone's taken my pen, but I don't know **who**.*
In replies: *"Where are you going?" "(I'm going to the) Library."*

blocks.text: In informal speech, the start of a sentence is often dropped (*situational ellipsis*): *(Have you) Seen Tom? / (It) Sounds good. / (I'll) See you later.* Don't use this in essays.

blocks.title: Ellipsis with auxiliaries: which one to keep?

blocks.text: Keep the **first** auxiliary from the original verb phrase:

items.en: "Have you been waiting long?" "Yes, I **have**."
He said it would be finished, and it **will (be)**.
"Should it have been sent?" "It **should have (been)**."

sections.title: so vs it, one vs it, do so vs do it

head: Compare
Meaning
Example
rows: I lost my umbrella, so I bought a new **one**.
I lost my umbrella, but then I found **it**.
Visitors wishing to leave early may **do so**.
informal, refers to a specific act
Don't touch the oven — I told you not to **do that**!

blocks.text: *Know*, *sure* and *certain* do not take *so*: ~~I know so~~ → *I know.* ~~I'm sure so~~ → *I'm sure (of it).*

items.en: ~~"Is she coming?" "I don't hope so."~~
items.note: *hope* forms the negative with **not**: *I hope not.*

items.en: ~~I prefer the red shoes to the black.~~
items.note: Fine in speech, but *ones* is needed when the noun is countable and not clear: *the black **ones***.

items.en: ~~I'd like a one with a balcony.~~
items.note: *a/an* + *one* needs an adjective: *a **big** one* — or just *one*.

items.en: ~~"Can you help?" "Yes, I can help it."~~
items.note: Use the auxiliary alone: *Yes, I can.*

items.en: ~~I didn't want to, but I had.~~

blocks.text: In academic writing, substitution prevents repetition and links sentences:

items.en: Many studies have examined online learning. **Those** that included adult learners reported higher drop-out rates.
The government promised to reduce emissions but has not **done so**.
Urban areas grew faster than rural **ones**.
Some participants improved; **others** did not.

blocks.text: *Do so*, *those* and *the former / the latter* are typical of formal writing. *Do it*, *that one* and situational ellipsis are typical of speech.
Replace nouns with **one(s)**, clauses with **so/not**, verb phrases with **do / an auxiliary / to**. Leave words out only when they are easy to recover.

items: *I hope not / I'm afraid not* — never *don't hope so*.
*I know / I'm sure* — never *know so*.
Formal: *do so, those, the former/latter*. Informal: dropped subjects (*Sounds great*).

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Future forms, probability and time clauses
summary: English has no single future tense. The form you choose shows how certain you are, whether something is planned or arranged, and how you see the action at a future moment.

blocks.text: Future meaning is expressed with modal verbs (*will, might*), present forms (*I'm meeting*, *the train leaves*) and semi-modals (*be going to, be about to, be due to*). Each adds a different shade of certainty or planning.

head: Form
Use
Example
rows: *Look at the sky, it**'s going to** rain.*
an action in progress at a future time; polite enquiries
*This time tomorrow I**'ll be flying** to Seoul.*

blocks.text: Use adverbs and phrases to show how likely something is:

head: Certainty
Expression
rows: *will definitely / is bound to / is sure to*
*will probably / is likely to / I expect*
*may / might / could / there's a chance that*
*probably won't / is unlikely to / I doubt whether*

blocks.text: Word order: *probably* comes after *will* but before *won't*: *She'll probably come* / *She probably won't come.*
After **when, as soon as, before, after, until, once, by the time** referring to the future, use a **present** tense, not *will*:

items.en: I'll call you **when** I **get** home.
~~I'll call you when I will get home.~~
Don't leave **until** you**'ve signed** the form.

blocks.text: The same rule applies to **if, unless, provided (that), as long as**.
Time expressions do not choose the future form for you — your **reason** (plan, arrangement, prediction, decision) does. But some expressions strongly prefer particular forms.

head: Expression
Typical form
Example
rows: **By Friday** I'**ll have finished** the draft.
**This time next week** we'**ll be lying** on a beach.
**One day** robots **will do** most of this.
**when, as soon as, until, before, after**
present tense in the time clause

items: *in two weeks* = at the end of that period: *I'll be back in two weeks.*
*within two weeks* = at some point before the end.
*by Friday* = no later than Friday (deadline).
*until Friday* = continuously up to Friday: *I'll be here until Friday.*

items.en: I**'ll** see Tom tomorrow.
I**'m going to** see Tom tomorrow.
I**'m seeing** Tom tomorrow.
**Will you be using** the car tonight?
**Will you use** the car tonight?
items.note: can sound like a request or demand

sections.title: Advanced usage: be + to, future in the past

items: **be about to** (very near future), **be on the point of / on the verge of** + -ing.
**be due to** for scheduled events: *The report is due to be published on Monday.*
**be to** for formal arrangements and instructions: *The president **is to** visit Paris next week. You **are to** report to reception.*
**Future in the past**: *I knew she **would** win. We **were going to** move, but…*
**will** for assumptions about the present: *That**'ll** be the postman.* (See *Uses of will and would*.)

items.en: ~~I will meet my dentist at four tomorrow.~~
items.note: Fixed arrangement → *I'm seeing my dentist at four.*

items.en: ~~When I will finish university, I'll travel.~~
~~She will probably not come.~~

blocks.text: Academic writing prefers impersonal forms of prediction: *It is likely that…*, *X is expected to…*, *X is projected to rise by 3%*. Formal notices use *be to* and *be due to*: *The building is due to reopen in spring.*

items: will = prediction/decision now; going to = intention/evidence; present continuous = arrangement; present simple = timetable.
Future continuous = in progress at a future time; future perfect = completed before it.
No *will* after time and condition conjunctions.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The future in the past: was going to, was to, was about to, would
summary: To talk about a past moment's future — plans, predictions, destinies and plans that failed — English shifts future forms into the past. The choice signals whether the future happened.

blocks.text: When we narrate or report, we often need to look forward from a point in the past: *In 1990 nobody knew that the internet **would** change everything.* *I **was going to** call you, but my phone died.* *She **was to** become the first woman to lead the institute.* These forms are the past-shifted versions of ordinary future forms. They allow a narrator to show plans, expectations, destinies and **unfulfilled intentions** with precision.

sections.title: How it works: a past viewpoint looking forward

blocks.text: Choose a reference point in the past, then take the future form you would have used at that point and **move it one step back**:

head: At the time (present viewpoint)
Narrated (past viewpoint)
rows: *He promised he **would** see me the next day.*
*The report is due to appear in May.*
*The report **was due to** appear in May.*

blocks.text: Whether the future event actually happened is often left open, or clarified by context or by the **perfect infinitive**: *We **were to have** met at noon* = the meeting was planned but did **not** happen.

*was/were going to* and *was/were to have + past participle* frequently imply that a plan was **not carried out**. *Would* and *was to* + base form, in narrative, often imply that the future **did** happen.

head: Form
Meaning
Example
rows: future seen from the past (prediction, promise)
past intention or prediction; often unfulfilled
*I **was going to** email you, but I forgot.*
was/were about to / on the point of + -ing
*I **was about to** leave when the phone rang. We **were on the point of giving** up.*
*It **was to** be his last film. We **were to** meet at six.*
*The minister **was to have** opened the bridge.*
*I couldn't come — I **was flying** to Rome the next day.*
completed before a future point in the past
*By the end of the year, he hoped, he **would have finished**.*

blocks.text: 1. Reporting predictions and promises
*Everyone thought the reforms **would** fail.* *She promised that she **would** be careful.*
2. Unfulfilled plans and excuses
*I **was going to** finish it last night, but ...* is the standard way to explain a plan that changed. Adding *but* clarifies.
3. Narrative foreshadowing (destiny)

*Was to* and *would* let a narrator reveal the future from a past viewpoint: *Little did he know that this meeting **would** change his life.* *The village **was to** remain isolated for another century.*
4. Interruptions of imminent action
*was about to / was on the point of / was just going to* + *when*: *We **were about to** sign the contract **when** the investor withdrew.*

items.en: At the time, few economists predicted that the crisis **would** spread so quickly.
I **was going to** apply for the scholarship, but the deadline had passed.
The building **was to have** opened in 2020, but construction stalled.
items.note: planned event that did not happen

items.en: Darwin **was to** spend five years on the voyage, a journey that **would** reshape biology.
She **was on the point of** resigning when she was offered a promotion.
The results **were due to** be published in March.
He hoped that by spring he **would have saved** enough for the trip.

head: Pair
Difference
rows: intention/plan (*I was going to tell you*) vs prediction or willingness seen from the past (*I knew you would understand*).
*was to do* vs *was to have done*
arrangement (outcome open, or destiny: it happened) vs arrangement that did not happen.
*I knew he would be late* (one future event) vs *Every day he would sit by the window* (past habit).
very soon vs at some point; *about to* is more imminent.
fixed arrangement (*I was meeting them at six*) vs intention (*I was going to meet them*).

blocks.text: *Was to* for destiny and *was to have done* for cancelled arrangements are formal and typical of historical narrative, biography and news. In conversation, *was going to* covers most cases.
Foreshadowing with *would* (*It would prove a costly mistake*) is a hallmark of narrative non-fiction and quality journalism; it creates suspense from hindsight.

items.en: ~~I knew she will pass the exam.~~
items.note: I knew she would pass the exam.

items.en: ~~I was going to call you but I have forgotten.~~
items.note: I was going to call you, but I forgot.

items.en: ~~The concert was to be held last week but was cancelled. (fine) / The concert was to held last week.~~
items.note: The concert was to be held last week.

items.en: ~~We were about leaving when it started raining.~~
items.note: We were about to leave when it started raining.

items.en: ~~The bridge was to open in 2020, but it didn't. (correct) / The bridge was to have open in 2020.~~
items.note: The bridge was to have opened in 2020.

items.en: ~~He said he is going to come, but he didn't.~~
items.note: He said he was going to come, but he didn't.

blocks.text: Foreshadowing for rhetorical effect
*It **was to prove** a turning point.* *This decision **would come back** to haunt the government.* Narrative hindsight adds drama to historical or analytical writing.
Hedged reporting of plans
*The agreement **was due to** be signed in June* reports a schedule without asserting it happened; useful when the outcome is uncertain.
Combining with negative inversion
*Little **did** they realise that the project **would** take a decade.* *Never **was** the empire **to** regain its former power.*

items: Move a future form one step back to look forward from a past point: *will → would, am going to → was going to, am to → was to*.
*Was going to* and *was to have done* often signal plans that did not happen.
*Would* and *was to* in narrative reveal what happened later (foreshadowing).
*Was about to / on the point of* + *when* for interrupted imminent actions.
*Would have done* = completion before a future point seen from the past.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Habits: used to, would, be used to and will
summary: Several structures talk about typical behaviour. They differ in time (past or present), in whether they describe states or actions, and in the attitude of the speaker.

blocks.text: Habitual forms describe things that happened regularly or were true for a long period. **used to** and **would** look back at past habits; **be/get used to** describes familiarity; **will** and **would** can describe typical (sometimes annoying) behaviour.

items.en: We **used to** live by the sea. Every summer we **would** swim before breakfast.

head: Structure
Form
Example
rows: didn't use to / Did you use to…?
*He **would** sit by the window for hours.*

blocks.text: In questions and negatives, *use to* has no *-d*: ~~Did you used to~~.

sections.title: Main rules: used to or would?

items: **used to** works for both **states and actions**: *I used to have long hair. I used to cycle to school.*
**would** works only for **repeated actions**, not states: ~~I would have long hair~~.
**would** normally needs a past time already established; it is common in nostalgic storytelling.
Use the **past simple** for a single past event or when you say how many times: *I went there twice*, not ~~I used to go there twice~~.

sections.title: be used to and get used to

blocks.text: These are completely different from *used to* + infinitive. They mean *be/become accustomed to* and are followed by a **noun or -ing form**:

items.en: She **isn't used to** driving on the left.
It took months to **get used to** the climate.
~~I'm used to get up early.~~
items.note: Use -ing: *I'm used to getting up early.*

sections.title: Typical and annoying behaviour: will, would, always + continuous

items: **will / would** (stressed in speech) for characteristic behaviour: *He'**ll** sit there for hours without saying a word.*
With stress, it shows irritation: *She **WOULD** say that!*
**always / constantly + continuous** for annoying habits: *You're always leaving the lights on!*

blocks.text: Habit markers (frequency adverbs, *every*, *whenever*) go with present simple or *used to/would* for the past. *These days* and *now* contrast present habits with past ones.

head: Expression
Example
rows: **in those days, back then, as a child**
**In those days** people **used to** write letters.
I **used to** smoke, but **these days** I **don't**.
She **no longer** works there. / She **doesn't** work there **any more**.

items.en: He's **always** borrowing my charger!

blocks.text: *Used to* and *would* need a past time frame. Don't use them with a specific number of times: ~~I used to visit Rome three times~~ → *I visited Rome three times.*

items.en: ~~I am used to live in a big city.~~
items.note: *I'm used to living…* (familiar) or *I used to live…* (past habit).

items.en: ~~I would have a dog when I was a child.~~
items.note: State → *I used to have a dog.*

items.en: ~~I use to go to the gym.~~
items.note: For present habits use the present simple: *I usually go…*

blocks.text: In formal writing, prefer *formerly*, *traditionally*, *in the past* or *tended to*: *Families traditionally ate together*; *Earlier studies tended to overlook gender.* *Would* for past habit is more literary and narrative.

items: used to: past states and habits that are no longer true.
would: repeated past actions only, in narrative.
be/get used to + -ing: be/become familiar with.
will/would/always + continuous: characteristic or annoying behaviour.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Indirect questions and question tags
summary: Indirect questions make requests and enquiries more polite; question tags check information and invite agreement. Both depend on getting word order and auxiliaries exactly right.

blocks.text: **Indirect questions** sound more polite and less direct. **Question tags** are short questions at the end of a statement, used to check facts or invite the listener to agree.

items.en: **Could you tell me where the station is?**
items.note: more polite than *Where is the station?*

items.en: You're from Kazan, **aren't you?**
It's a lovely day, **isn't it?**

blocks.text: Indirect questions
After the introductory phrase, use **statement word order** (subject + verb) and no *do/does/did*.

head: Direct question
Indirect question
rows: Could you tell me where **the station is**?
Do you know what time **it opens**?
I'd like to know how much **it costs**.

blocks.text: Common introductions: *Could you tell me…? / Do you know…? / I was wondering… / Would you mind telling me…? / Have you any idea…? / I'd like to know…*
Yes/no questions need **if** or **whether**: *Do you know **if** the museum is open?*
Question tags
Positive statement → **negative tag**; negative statement → **positive tag**. Use the same auxiliary (or *do/does/did*) and a pronoun.

head: Statement
Tag
Note
rows: *nobody, nothing, never* are negative → positive tag

items: **Falling** intonation on a tag: you are fairly sure and expect agreement. *It's cold, ↘isn't it?*
**Rising** intonation: a real question; you're not sure. *You're coming, ↗aren't you?*
**Same-polarity tags** (positive + positive) show interest, surprise or sarcasm: *So you're the new manager, **are you**?*
Indirect questions are used for politeness, in formal emails and in interviews: *I was wondering whether you could send me the agenda.*

blocks.text: *I was wondering if…* and *Would you mind telling me…* are the most polite. *Any idea…?* is informal.

head: Indirect question (now, polite)
Reported question (telling what someone asked)
rows: Can you tell me if **it's** free?

blocks.text: Both use statement word order; reported questions usually also **backshift** the tense.

items.en: ~~Could you tell me where is the station?~~
~~Do you know what time does the film start?~~
~~I wonder are they coming.~~
~~You haven't seen my keys, haven't you?~~
~~I'm late, am not I?~~
**What** she said I can't remember.
items.note: A *wh*-clause as the object, fronted for emphasis.

items.en: It's anyone's guess **whether** the deal will go ahead.
**Whether** we like it or not, prices will rise.
items.note: *whether … or not* = it doesn't matter if

items.en: I'd be grateful if you could let me know **when** the results will be available.

blocks.text: In formal writing prefer *whether* to *if*, and always use *whether* after prepositions and before *to*-infinitives: *a debate about **whether** to ban cars* (~~about if~~).
Indirect questions: polite opener + (wh-word / if / whether) + **subject + verb**. Tags: opposite polarity, same auxiliary, pronoun subject.

items: *I'm…, aren't I? / Let's…, shall we? / Nobody…, did they?*
Falling tag = expecting agreement; rising tag = real question.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Emphasis: cleft sentences, inversion, fronting and auxiliary do
summary: English normally puts new or important information at the end of a sentence. Clefts, inversion, fronting and emphatic do let you control what the reader notices, which is essential for persuasive speaking and writing.

blocks.text: Emphasis structures change the normal order of information to highlight one part of the message. They are typical of persuasive essays, presentations and careful conversation.

head: Type
Pattern
Example
rows: ***It was the cost that** surprised me.*
***All I want is** a quiet weekend.*
***The reason (why) I left was** the pay.*

items.en: **It wasn't until** midnight **that** they finally agreed.
items.note: *It was not until…* = only at that time

blocks.text: Stressed *do/does/did* before the main verb contradicts or confirms strongly:

items.en: I **did** send the email, I promise!
She **does** work hard, even if it doesn't look like it.
**Do** sit down.

sections.title: Inversion after negative and limiting adverbials

blocks.text: When a negative or restrictive expression comes first, use **question word order** (auxiliary + subject):

head: Adverbial
Example
rows: ***Not only did** she win, **but** she **also** broke the record.*
***No sooner had** we arrived **than** it started to rain.*
Only then / Only after / Only when
***Only when** the results came **did we realise** our mistake.*
Under no circumstances / On no account
***Under no circumstances should you** share your password.*
***Little did they know** what was coming.*
***So severe was** the damage **that** the bridge closed.*

blocks.text: With *Only after / Only when / Not until*, invert the **main** clause, not the time clause: *Only when I got home **did I notice** the cut.*

items: **Fronting** moves an element to the start for contrast or emphasis: ***This** I cannot accept. **Strange** as it may seem, he was right.*
**Tailing** adds the topic at the end in speech: *It's lovely, **that beach**.* *He's very clever, **your brother**.*
**Concessive fronting**: *Much as I admire her, I disagree. Try as he might, he couldn't open it.*

items.en: I've never seen such chaos.
Never have I seen such chaos.
Jack broke the window.
It was Jack who broke the window.
What Jack did was break the window.
~~Never I have seen such a mess.~~
~~Not only she sings, but she also dances.~~
~~Only when I got home I noticed the cut.~~

blocks.text: Inversion is formal and should be used sparingly in essays, typically once or twice for impact, especially in introductions and conclusions: *Not only does tourism create jobs, but it also funds conservation.* Clefts are useful in academic writing to signal contrast: *It is this assumption that the present study challenges.*

items: It-clefts and what-clefts move focus.
Emphatic *do* confirms or contradicts.
Negative/limiting adverbial first → auxiliary + subject.
Fronting and tailing for contrast and spoken style.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Linking ideas: contrast, concession, cause and result
summary: Linkers show the logical relationship between ideas. Using the right one, with the right grammar after it, is essential for coherent essays and arguments.

blocks.text: Linking devices connect clauses and sentences: contrast (*however*), concession (*although*), cause (*because of*), result (*therefore*), addition (*moreover*). Each belongs to a grammatical type, which decides what follows it.

head: Type
Followed by
Examples
rows: *although, even though, while, whereas, because, so*
*despite, in spite of, because of, due to, owing to*
a new sentence (often after a full stop or semicolon)

items.en: **Although** it was raining, we went out.
**Despite** the rain / **Despite** it raining, we went out.
It was raining. **However**, we went out.

items: **while / whereas** contrast two facts: *The north is wet, **whereas** the south is dry.*
**although / even though / though** concede a point: ***Even though** he was ill, he finished the race.* (*even though* is stronger)
**despite / in spite of** + noun / -ing / *the fact that*: ***Despite the fact that** prices rose, sales increased.*
**however / nevertheless / nonetheless / even so** start a new sentence.
**Adverbials of concession** (C1): *admittedly, granted, all the same, be that as it may*.

head: Cause
Result
rows: so, so … that, such … that (+ clause)
because of, due to, owing to, as a result of (+ noun)
therefore, consequently, as a result, thus, hence (sentence adverbs)

items.en: The match was cancelled **due to** heavy rain.
The rain was heavy. **Consequently**, the match was cancelled.

blocks.text: *Due to* traditionally follows *be*: *The delay was due to fog.* In formal writing, prefer *owing to / because of* at the start of a sentence.
*Moreover, Furthermore, In addition, What is more, Besides* add points; *provided that, as long as, unless* add conditions (see *Conditionals*).

items.en: Although it was late, …
~~Although of the late hour, …~~
On the other hand…
items.note: introduces the other side of an argument

items.en: On the contrary…
items.note: says the previous idea is false: *It wasn't boring. On the contrary, it was fascinating.*

items.en: ~~Despite of the weather, we went.~~
items.note: *Despite the weather* / *In spite of the weather*.

items.en: ~~Although he was tired, but he continued.~~
items.note: Use one linker only: *Although he was tired, he continued.*

items.en: ~~The economy grew, however unemployment rose.~~
items.note: *however* starts a new sentence or follows a semicolon: *…grew; however, unemployment rose.*

items: Fronted concession: ***Much as** I admire the plan, it is unrealistic.* ***Difficult though** it may be, we must act.*
*Whereas* and *while* can begin the sentence for balanced contrast.
Overusing *Moreover/Furthermore* at the start of every sentence sounds mechanical; vary with *This also…, A further problem is…*.

blocks.text: Formal: *nevertheless, consequently, thus, hence, notwithstanding*. Neutral: *however, therefore, although*. Informal: *but, so, anyway, still*. Good essays use a range, placed naturally, and not at the start of every sentence.

items: Conjunction + clause; preposition + noun/-ing; sentence adverb + new sentence.
*although/even though* vs *despite/in spite of*.
*because* + clause vs *because of/due to* + noun.
*on the other hand* (other side) vs *on the contrary* (rejecting).

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Modals: obligation, deduction and stance
summary: Modal verbs and modal expressions show how certain, necessary or permitted something is. At C1, modality also means signalling your stance with adjectives, adverbs and nouns.

blocks.text: Modality expresses the speaker's attitude to a statement. Two main areas:

items: **Obligation and permission** (deontic): *must, have to, should, can, be allowed to, needn't*.
**Probability and deduction** (epistemic): *must, can't, might, could, may, should, will*.

blocks.text: Modal verbs (*can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would*) take a bare infinitive, have no *-s* and form questions by inversion. Semi-modals (*have to, need to, be able to, ought to, be supposed to*) behave more like normal verbs.

head: Meaning
Forms
rows: *don't have to, needn't, don't need to*
*mustn't, can't, aren't allowed to, be forbidden to*
*can, may (formal), be allowed to, be permitted to*

items.en: You **mustn't** smoke here.
You **don't have to** come.
We **didn't need to** pay.
items.note: it wasn't necessary (we probably didn't pay)

items.en: We **needn't have paid**.
items.note: we paid, but it wasn't necessary

items.en: She's not answering. She **must be** in a meeting.
He **can't have taken** the train; there were no trains that night.

blocks.text: The negative of deductive *must* is *can't*, not ~~mustn't~~: *That can't be right.*

items.en: You **should have told** me.
You **could have told** me.
items.note: reproach: it was possible but you didn't

items.en: **Could** you swim when you were five?
I **managed to / was able to** escape.
You **had better** leave now.
items.note: strong advice with a warning; refers to now or the future

sections.title: Advanced usage: modality beyond modal verbs

blocks.text: At C1 you can express the same meanings more precisely with other structures:

items: adjectives: *It is **highly unlikely** that…*, *It is **essential** that…*, *X is **bound/liable/apt** to…*
adverbs: *conceivably, presumably, inevitably, arguably*
nouns: *There is **every likelihood** that…*, *There's **no question of**…*, *in all probability*
verbs: *It **remains to be seen** whether…*, *The data **suggest** that…*

items.en: **In all likelihood**, the trial will be postponed.
It is **imperative** that every passenger **wear** a seat belt.
~~You mustn't to wear a tie.~~
items.note: No *to* after modals: *You don't have to wear a tie* (if you mean no obligation).

items.en: ~~He must have been at home yesterday, I'm not sure.~~
items.note: *must* = certainty; use *might have been* if unsure.

items.en: ~~I could finish the marathon last year.~~

blocks.text: Academic writing uses modality to **hedge** claims: *These findings **may** indicate…*, *This **could** be explained by…*, *It **would seem** that…*. Strong modals (*must, certainly*) are reserved for well-supported claims. Formal rules use *be required to, be prohibited from, be permitted to*.

items: Obligation: must/have to; no obligation: don't have to/needn't; prohibition: mustn't.
Deduction: must (sure), can't (sure not), might/could (possible); past = modal + have + V3.
*needn't have done* = did it unnecessarily; *didn't need to do* = it wasn't necessary.
At C1, use adjectives, adverbs and nouns of likelihood to state your stance precisely.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Multi-word verbs: phrasal and prepositional verbs, word order and register
summary: "Look up a word" and "look at a word" look alike but behave differently. Knowing the grammar of multi-word verbs lets you place objects correctly, form passives and nouns, and choose between a phrasal verb and a formal single-word verb.

blocks.text: English has thousands of verbs made of a verb plus a particle: *give up, look into, put up with, carry out*. They are not one category but three, and their grammar differs: where the object can go, whether the particle is stressed, and whether they can be passivised. Advanced users also need to know when a phrasal verb is the natural choice and when a formal equivalent is better.

sections.title: How it works: adverb particles and prepositions

blocks.text: The particle after the verb is either an **adverb** (*up, out, away, back, down, off*) or a **preposition** (*at, for, into, with, on*).

items: **Phrasal verbs** (verb + adverb particle): the particle belongs to the verb and changes its meaning: *give up* (stop), *turn down* (refuse). The particle can usually move: *turn down **the offer** / turn **the offer** down*.
**Prepositional verbs** (verb + preposition): the preposition belongs to the object noun phrase: *look **at the chart**, rely **on volunteers***. The object always follows the preposition.
**Phrasal-prepositional verbs** (verb + adverb + preposition): *put up **with**, look forward **to**, come up **with**, get away **with***. The object follows the whole sequence.

blocks.text: A pronoun object goes **between** the verb and the adverb particle of a phrasal verb: *turn **it** down* (~~turn down it~~), but **after** the preposition of a prepositional verb: *look **at it***.

head: Type
Object position
Example
Passive
rows: before or after particle; pronoun before

blocks.text: Stress
Adverb particles are usually stressed: *She turned it **DOWN**.* Prepositions are usually unstressed: *She **LOOKED** at it.*
Long objects
With a long object, put the particle first: *They turned **down** every proposal that the committee had submitted* (not *turned every proposal ... down*).
1. Literal, aspectual and idiomatic meaning

items: **Literal**: *take the boxes **out***.
**Aspectual** (the particle adds completion, continuation or beginning): *eat **up**, use **up*** (completely); *carry **on**, keep **on*** (continue); *set **off**, start **up*** (begin).
**Idiomatic**: *put off* (postpone), *come across* (find by chance), *bring about* (cause).

blocks.text: 2. Nouns and adjectives from phrasal verbs

*break down → a breakdown; turn out → the turnout; set back → a setback; cut back → cutbacks; drop out → a dropout; outcome, outbreak, input, upkeep, follow-up, built-up area, worn-out shoes.* These nouns are common even in formal writing.
3. Register choice

Many phrasal verbs have a Latinate equivalent: *find out / discover, put off / postpone, set up / establish, look into / investigate, carry out / conduct, go up / increase, point out / indicate.* Phrasal verbs are natural in speech and most journalism; academic writing often prefers the single verb, but some phrasal verbs are fully academic: *carry out, point out, set out, account for, rule out, draw on, bring about*.

items.en: The researchers **carried out** a series of interviews.
items.note: academic phrasal verb, natural in formal writing

items.en: We need to **rule out** other explanations before drawing conclusions.
I **came across** an interesting article; I'll send it **over**.
The proposal was **turned down** because it was too expensive.
items.note: passive of a separable phrasal verb

items.en: You shouldn't **put up with** that kind of behaviour.
The strike led to a major **setback** for the negotiations.
The decline **can be accounted for** by changes in demand.
items.note: passive prepositional verb in academic style

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *look up a word* vs *look up the street*
phrasal (search for: *look it up*) vs verb + prepositional phrase (direction: *look up it* is impossible; *look up the street* = towards).
prepositional (visit / formally ask: *call on someone*) vs phrasal (phone; summon: *call someone up*).
same meaning; *turn down* is neutral/informal, *refuse/decline* more formal.
*get over* an illness or disappointment (recover); *overcome* a difficulty (formal, effort).
invent (*make up a story*), constitute (*women make up 60%*), reconcile (*they made up*), compensate (*make up for lost time*). Context decides.

blocks.text: Informal phrasal verbs such as *get on with, mess up, sort out, chuck out* belong in speech and informal writing. In essays, prefer *proceed, spoil, resolve, discard* — but do not replace academic phrasal verbs like *carry out, point out, account for* with odd formal equivalents.
Overly formal single verbs in conversation sound stiff: *We must postpone the meeting* is fine at work, but among friends *Let's put it off* is more natural.

items.en: ~~I looked up it in the dictionary.~~
items.note: I looked it up in the dictionary.

items.en: ~~She is looking forward to meet you.~~
items.note: She is looking forward to meeting you. (*to* is a preposition)

items.en: ~~Can you pick up me at eight?~~
items.note: Can you pick me up at eight?

items.en: ~~They called off it because of the rain.~~
items.note: They called it off because of the rain.

items.en: ~~We need to discuss about the problem.~~
items.note: We need to discuss the problem. (no preposition)

items.en: ~~The data was carried by the team out.~~
items.note: The data were collected by the team. / The analysis was carried out by the team.

blocks.text: Particles with consistent meanings

Learning particle meanings speeds up acquisition: **up** = completion or increase (*fill up, step up, scale up*); **down** = reduction or recording (*scale down, write down, narrow down*); **out** = to the end or outward (*sort out, wear out, phase out*); **off** = separation or cancellation (*call off, cut off, write off*); **through** = to completion (*follow through, see through*).
Academic phrasal verbs worth mastering
*account for, bear out, build on, carry out, draw on, embark on, factor in, point out, rule out, set out, single out, spell out, stem from, weigh up.*
Particle placement for emphasis
In speech the object can follow the particle for end-focus even if short: *He gave back **the money** — all of it.* But with pronouns, separation remains obligatory.

items: Phrasal verbs: verb + adverb particle; object can separate; pronouns go in the middle.
Prepositional verbs: verb + preposition; object always after the preposition.
Phrasal-prepositional verbs: object after both particles (*put up with it*).
Many phrasal verbs form nouns (*setback, outcome, breakdown*).
Choose register carefully: some phrasal verbs are academic, others are informal.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Narrative tenses and the past perfect
summary: Telling a story in English means choosing between past simple, past continuous, past perfect and past perfect continuous to show order, background and cause.

blocks.text: Narrative tenses organise a story in time. The **past simple** moves the story forward; the **past continuous** describes the background; the **past perfect** steps back to an earlier event; the **past perfect continuous** shows an activity that continued up to a past moment.

items.en: It **was raining** and the streets **were** empty. I **had been walking** for an hour when I **realised** I **had left** my keys at the office.

head: Tense
Form
Function in a story
rows: duration up to a past moment, causes

items: Use the **past perfect** only when you need to make the earlier time clear. If events are told in order, the past simple is enough: *I got up, had a shower and left.*
Use it after **time conjunctions** when the order matters: *When I arrived, the film started* (I arrived, then it started) vs *When I arrived, the film had started* (it started before).
With **before, after, as soon as**, the past perfect is optional because the conjunction already shows the order.
Use the **past perfect continuous** to explain a visible result in the past: *Her eyes were red: she had been crying.*

blocks.text: Linkers show the order of events; the tense shows how the speaker sees them. Choose the linker first, then check the tense.

head: Expression
Typical tense
Example
rows: **While** we **were packing**, the lights went out.
**By the time** we arrived, the film **had started**.
**for, since** (looking back from a past point)
**then, next, eventually, in the end, at last**

items.en: **No sooner had** we sat down **than** the phone rang.
items.note: Inverted pattern for emphasis — see *Inversion and emphasis*.

items.en: **Hardly** had she arrived **when** the trouble began.

blocks.text: *After* and *before* already show order, so the past perfect is optional: *After she (had) left, I called him.*

items.en: When she came in, we **had** dinner.
items.note: She came in, then we ate.

items.en: When she came in, we **were having** dinner.
items.note: We were in the middle of dinner.

items.en: When she came in, we **had had** dinner.
I **had read** the book twice.
I **had been reading** for hours.

sections.title: Other ways to talk about the past

items: **used to / would** for past habits (see *Habits: used to and would*).
**was going to / was about to** for plans that did not happen: *I was going to call you, but I forgot.*
**The historic present**: storytellers and journalists sometimes use present tenses to make a past story vivid: *So I'm walking home, and this man stops me…* (informal speech, C1).

items.en: ~~After I had finished, I had gone home.~~
items.note: Only the earlier action needs the past perfect: *After I had finished, I went home.*

items.en: ~~I was knowing the answer.~~
~~Yesterday I had met an old friend.~~
items.note: No earlier past reference point: *Yesterday I met an old friend.*

items: Writers use the past perfect for **flashbacks**, then return to the past simple once the earlier time is established, to avoid a long chain of *had*.
**Hardly / No sooner** with the past perfect and inversion (formal): *No sooner had we sat down than the alarm went off.* (See *Inversion and emphasis*.)
**Perfect infinitives** for reported past: *He is said to have left the country.*

blocks.text: In historical and academic narratives, the past perfect frames background before the main period: *By 1900, the city's population had doubled.* Avoid the historic present in formal essays unless you are summarising a literary plot, where the present simple is standard: *In the novel, the protagonist returns home…*

items: Past simple moves the story; continuous gives background; perfect steps back.
Use the past perfect only where order would otherwise be unclear.
Past perfect continuous explains causes and duration up to a past point.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Negation, scope and focusing adverbs: not, no, hardly, only, even
summary: Where you put "not" or "only" decides what you are denying or highlighting. Advanced English uses negative transfer, negative quantifiers and understatement to make claims precise and tactful.

blocks.text: *All the students didn't pass* and *Not all the students passed* look similar but can mean different things. *I don't think it's fair* is more natural than *I think it isn't fair*. *Only* in different positions changes the claim. This lesson is about **what** a negative or focusing word applies to — its **scope** — and the conventions English uses to negate politely and precisely.

sections.title: How it works: scope and focus

blocks.text: A negative or focusing word affects the part of the sentence that follows it and falls within its **scope**. Compare:

items.en: She **deliberately didn't** answer.
She **didn't deliberately** answer.

blocks.text: In speech, stress marks the focus: *I didn't say she **stole** the money* (I said something else about the money) vs *I didn't say **she** stole the money* (someone else did). In writing, there is no stress, so **word order** and **choice of structure** must make the scope clear.
Put a negative or focusing word as close as possible to the element it applies to. When in doubt, restructure: *Not all of the data were usable* is clearer than *All of the data weren't usable*.
Negative forms

head: Form
Example
Note
rows: *We don't have **any** data. I didn't go **either**.*
***None of** the samples was / were contaminated.*
***Neither** option is ideal. She didn't agree, **nor** did I.*
one negative per clause in standard English
negative meaning; take positive tags: *..., do we?*
negative: "not much/many" (*a little, a few* are positive)

blocks.text: Focusing adverbs

head: Adverb
Position and meaning
