rows: before the focused element in writing: *We **only** tested **adults*** (ambiguous) → *We tested **only adults*** (precise)
adds surprise: ***Even** experts disagree. They didn't **even** reply.*
= only/exactly: *It's **just** a theory. That's **just** what I meant.*
restrict to a subset: *The effect was strong, **particularly among** older users.*

blocks.text: 1. Negative transfer (raising)

With *think, believe, suppose, expect, imagine, seem, appear*, English normally negates the main verb, not the clause: *I **don't think** he's right* (not *I think he isn't right*), *It **doesn't seem** likely.* This sounds less direct and more polite.
2. Partial versus total negation
***Not all** respondents agreed* = some did not. ***No** respondents agreed / **None** of the respondents agreed* = zero agreement. *All respondents didn't agree* is ambiguous; avoid it in writing.
3. Understatement (litotes)

Negating a negative adjective gives a cautious positive: *not uncommon* (fairly common), *not unreasonable*, *not insignificant*, *not without problems*. Very common in academic and diplomatic English.
4. Negative tags and responses
After negative adverbs, use positive tags: *She **seldom** complains, **does** she?* Responses agree with the negative: *"I can't swim." "**Neither** can I." / "Nor can I." / "Me neither."*

items.en: I **don't believe** the figures have been checked.
**Not every** policy that sounds fair is fair in practice.
There is **little** evidence to support this claim.
The results are **not insignificant**.
items.note: litotes: cautious way to say *quite significant*

items.en: **Only** later did the team realise the error.
The change affected **only** part-time staff.
He **didn't even** apologise.
items.note: *even* stresses that the minimum expected action was missing

head: Pair
Difference
rows: negative (*little time* = not enough) vs positive (*a little time* = some). Same for *few / a few*.
*no* + noun is more emphatic: *It's **no** surprise* vs *It's **not a** surprise*. *Not* before adjectives: *not easy*.
*I didn't see anyone* = *I saw no one* (formal). Never *~~I didn't see no one~~* in standard English.
*hardly* = almost not; *hard* = with effort. *Hardly any/ever* = almost none/never.
positive addition *also/too*; negative addition *either*: *I don't like it **either*** (~~too~~).

blocks.text: Formal: *no, none, neither, nor, scarcely, seldom, little, few*. Neutral/informal: *not any, not ... either, hardly, me neither*. Double negatives (*I don't know nothing*) are features of some dialects and informal speech, but non-standard in writing.
Litotes and negative transfer are key politeness devices in British English: *That's **not the best** idea* often means *That's a bad idea*. Be aware of this when interpreting feedback.

items.en: ~~I think it isn't a good idea.~~
items.note: I don't think it's a good idea.

items.en: ~~All the students didn't pass the exam. (meaning some failed)~~
items.note: Not all the students passed the exam.

items.en: ~~I don't like coffee too.~~
~~He hardly didn't sleep.~~
~~Few people came, so it was crowded.~~
items.note: Few people came, so it was quiet. / A few people came ... (meaning changes)

items.en: ~~None of us have no idea.~~
items.note: None of us has any idea. / None of us have any idea.

blocks.text: Negative inversion for rhetoric
***Under no circumstances** should the data be shared. **Not only** was it late, it was incomplete. **At no point** did the minister apologise.* (See the inversion lesson.)
Scope in academic claims

*This does **not necessarily** mean ...* / *This **necessarily does not** mean ...*: the first denies necessity (it may or may not mean it); the second asserts a necessary negative. Precision here matters in argument.
Focusing adverbs with numbers
*The scheme reached **just** 12% of eligible households* (= a disappointingly small number) vs *as many as 12%* (= surprisingly large). The adverb carries the writer's evaluation.

items: Place *not, only, even* close to what they affect; restructure to avoid ambiguous scope.
Prefer negative transfer: *I don't think X* rather than *I think not-X*.
*Not all* = partial; *no/none* = total.
*Little/few* are negative, *a little/a few* positive.
Use litotes (*not uncommon*) for cautious claims; use positive tags after *hardly, seldom*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Noun clauses: that-clauses, wh-clauses and whether
summary: A noun clause does the job of a noun: it can be the subject, object or complement of a sentence. Noun clauses let you package whole ideas, which is essential for argument and academic writing.

blocks.text: Compare *I understand **the problem*** with *I understand **why the system failed***. The clause *why the system failed* fills the same position as the noun phrase *the problem*. That is a **noun clause** (also called a nominal or content clause). Noun clauses let you treat a statement, a question or a fact as a single unit you can then describe, evaluate or argue about: ***What the data show** is **that** the effect is temporary.*

sections.title: How it works: three families of noun clause

blocks.text: 1. **That-clauses** package a statement: *(that) the experiment worked*. 2. **Wh-clauses** package an open question or an unknown: *what happened, why prices rose, how the scheme works*. 3. **Whether/if-clauses** package a yes/no question: *whether the policy is fair*. Because they are no longer real questions, wh- and whether-clauses use **statement word order**: *I wonder why **she left*** (not *~~why did she leave~~*). This is the same logic as indirect questions.

Noun clauses can stand where nouns stand: **subject** (*That he resigned surprised everyone*), **object** (*I doubt whether it matters*), **complement** (*The problem is that we lack data*), **after a preposition** (*It depends on **what** you mean*) and **in apposition** to a noun (*the fact **that** he lied*).

head: Position
That-clause
Wh-clause
Whether-clause
rows: ***Whether** it works* remains to be seen.
The question is **whether** we can afford it.
It depends on **how** you do it.

blocks.text: *That* can be omitted after common reporting verbs and adjectives in informal style (*I think you're right*), but not when the clause is the subject (***That** he lied is obvious*).
1. Packaging an idea as the topic

Starting with a noun clause puts the idea in focus: ***How** universities should be funded** is a recurring debate.* Long subject clauses are often moved to the end with anticipatory *it* (see that lesson): *It is unclear **whether** the scheme works.*
2. Reporting and evaluating

Reporting verbs (*argue, claim, suggest, demonstrate*) take that-clauses; verbs of uncertainty (*wonder, ask, doubt, investigate, establish*) take wh- or whether-clauses: *The study investigates **whether** sleep affects recall.*
3. Talking about facts with prepositions

Prepositions cannot be followed directly by a that-clause. Use ***the fact that***: *Despite **the fact that** it rained, ...*; *She was annoyed **by the fact that** nobody replied.* (Or rephrase: *Although it rained ...*)
4. Nominal relative clauses
*What, whatever, whoever, wherever* create clauses meaning "the thing(s) that / anyone who": *I'll do **whatever** it takes.* These are covered in detail in the lesson on nominal relative clauses.

items.en: **That** the climate is changing is no longer disputed.
It is no longer disputed **that** the climate is changing.
The report does not explain **how** the figures were calculated.
Much depends on **whether** the government acts quickly.
items.note: whether-clause after a preposition (*if* is not possible here)

items.en: The assumption **that** growth is always good needs examining.
I'm not convinced **(that)** this is the right approach.
**Why** some languages die out while others thrive is a complex question.

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *the news **that** she had won* (= content of the news; *that* cannot be replaced by *which*) vs *the news **that/which** she brought* (relative: *that* is the object of *brought*).

Both introduce yes/no clauses after verbs (*I don't know whether/if ...*). Only *whether* is possible: as subject, after prepositions, before *to*-infinitive (*whether to go*) and with *or not* immediately after (*whether or not*).
*what* = the thing which: *What he said was true.* *That* introduces a fact: *That he said it was true* (= the fact of his saying it).
*Do you know where **she lives**?* not *~~where does she live~~*.
After prepositions and as a heavy subject, *the fact that* is required or clearer.

blocks.text: Subject that-clauses (*That X is true is clear*) are formal and can sound heavy; most writers prefer *It is clear that X*. Subject wh-clauses (*What matters is ...*) are common in both speech and writing as a focusing device.
Overuse of *the fact that* makes prose wordy: *Due to the fact that* → *because*; *In spite of the fact that* → *although*. Keep it where a noun phrase is genuinely needed.

items.en: ~~I don't know what does he want.~~
items.note: I don't know what he wants.

items.en: ~~Despite that it was late, we continued.~~
items.note: Despite the fact that it was late, ... / Although it was late, ...

items.en: ~~The question is if we should continue.~~
items.note: The question is whether we should continue.

items.en: ~~What I want to say that education matters.~~
items.note: What I want to say is that education matters.

items.en: ~~I'm not sure about if it is correct.~~
items.note: I'm not sure whether it is correct.

items.en: ~~The news which he had resigned shocked everyone.~~
items.note: The news that he had resigned shocked everyone.

blocks.text: Pseudo-clefts with noun clauses

***What** the evidence suggests **is that** the effect fades over time.* The wh-clause sets up expectation; the that-clause delivers the point. This structure is powerful in conclusions but loses force if repeated.
Mandative that-clauses
After verbs and nouns of demand and recommendation, formal English uses the base form: *The committee recommends **that** the policy **be** reviewed.* (See the subjunctive lesson.)
Noun clauses and hedging

Embedding a claim in a that-clause lets you attribute and qualify it: *It **appears** that ..., There is **some evidence** that ..., One **possible** explanation is that ...*. This is a central technique of academic stance.

items: Noun clauses function as subject, object, complement, prepositional object or appositive.
That-clauses report facts and claims; wh- and whether-clauses report unknowns and questions.
Use statement word order inside wh- and whether-clauses.
After prepositions use wh-/whether-clauses or *the fact that*, never a bare that-clause.
*Whether* (not *if*) as subject, after prepositions, before to-infinitives and with *or not*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Participle clauses and reduced relative clauses
summary: Participle clauses compress information: they replace a full clause with an -ing, -ed or having + past participle form. They make writing denser and more formal, and they also reduce relative clauses.

blocks.text: A participle clause is a clause without a subject and without a full verb. It is built on a **present participle** (*-ing*), a **past participle** (*-ed / V3*) or a **perfect participle** (*having + V3*). It can describe time, reason, result, condition or add information about a noun.

items.en: **Feeling tired**, she went to bed early.
The man **sitting by the window** is my tutor.

head: Form
Meaning
Example
rows: ***Built** in 1890, the bridge is still in use.*
***Not knowing** what to do, I called my mother.*

sections.title: Adverbial participle clauses: time, reason, result, condition

items.en: **After graduating**, she moved to Toronto.
**Being** the eldest, he had to look after the others.
The storm destroyed the bridge, **cutting off** the village.
**Used** correctly, the device is completely safe.
**While waiting** for the bus, I read the news.

blocks.text: A defining or non-defining relative clause can often be reduced:

head: Full relative clause
Reduced
rows: The woman **who is speaking** is a judge.
The first person **to arrive**… (infinitive after *first, last, only*, superlatives)

blocks.text: Use *-ing* for active meaning even with past events: *The man **driving** the car was injured* (who was driving). Do not reduce with the perfect: ~~The people having attended~~ → *The people who had attended*.

items.en: The people **interviewing** the candidates…
The people **interviewed** for the study…
**Opening** the door, she saw the parcel.
**Having opened** the door, she went back to the kitchen.
~~Walking down the street, the rain started.~~
items.note: Dangling participle: the subject of the main clause must be the one doing the participle. *Walking down the street, I got caught in the rain.*

items.en: ~~Having lived in Paris, she lives there for ten years.~~
items.note: Wrong logic: *Having lived in Paris for ten years, she speaks fluent French.*

items.en: ~~The books writing by him are popular.~~

items: Participle clauses with their own subject (absolute constructions, formal/literary): ***The work finished**, we went home.* ***Weather permitting**, the match will go ahead.*
Fixed participle expressions: *generally speaking, judging by, considering, given (that), assuming (that), provided*.
*With* + noun + participle: ***With prices rising**, families are cutting back.*

blocks.text: Participle clauses are common in academic, journalistic and descriptive writing: *Drawing on survey data, this study examines… / Compared with 2010, unemployment has fallen.* In conversation, full clauses are more natural.

items: -ing = active; V3 = passive; having + V3 = earlier action.
They replace adverbial clauses (time, reason, condition, result) and relative clauses.
The implied subject must match the main clause subject.
*first/last/only* + to-infinitive in reduced relatives.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The passive, impersonal passives and the causative
summary: The passive lets you choose what a sentence is about and leave out who did the action. Advanced forms include impersonal reporting passives, passive infinitives and -ing forms, get-passives and causatives.

blocks.text: In an active sentence the subject does the action; in a passive sentence the subject **receives** it. Use the passive when the agent is unknown, obvious, unimportant, or when you want to keep the focus on a topic already mentioned.

items.en: The bridge **was built** in 1890.
items.note: who built it is not important here

items.en: Penicillin was discovered in 1928. It **was later developed** into a mass-produced drug.

blocks.text: *be* (in the correct tense) + past participle.

head: Tense
Passive
rows: will be made / must be made / should have been made
to be made / to have been made / being made / having been made

blocks.text: Add the agent with *by* only when it is new or important: *The novel was written **by a 19-year-old**.*
With verbs such as *say, believe, think, report, expect, know, consider, allege*, there are two patterns:

head: Pattern
Example
rows: ***It is believed that*** the painting is a fake.
*The painting **is believed to be** a fake.*
*The thieves **are thought to have escaped** by boat.*
*The minister **is said to be considering** resigning.*

items.en: Nobody likes **being criticised** in public.
The forms need **to be signed** by Friday.
She expects **to have been promoted** by then.
He **got fired** for being late.
items.note: get-passive: informal; often sudden or unwelcome events

blocks.text: *need + -ing* has passive meaning in British English: *The car needs washing* = needs to be washed.

sections.title: The causative: have and get something done

blocks.text: Use **have/get + object + past participle** when you arrange for someone else to do something, or when something unpleasant happens to you:

items.en: I'm **having my hair cut** tomorrow.
items.note: I pay someone to cut it

items.en: She **got her bag stolen** on the train.

blocks.text: Related active patterns: **have someone do** (*I had the mechanic check the brakes*), **get someone to do** (*I got my brother to help me*).

items.en: I cut my hair.
I had my hair cut.
The report was written last week.
The report got written in the end.
~~The meeting was happened on Monday.~~
items.note: Intransitive verbs (*happen, arrive, die, occur*) have no passive.

items.en: ~~It is said that he to be rich.~~
items.note: Mix of two patterns: *It is said that he is rich* / *He is said to be rich*.

items.en: ~~I must repair my car tomorrow at the garage.~~
items.note: If someone else does it: *I must have/get my car repaired.*

blocks.text: Academic and scientific writing uses the passive to focus on processes and results: *Samples were collected from 40 sites and analysed.* Impersonal passives distance the writer from claims: *It has been argued that…*, *X is widely regarded as…*. Don't overuse it: a mix of active and passive reads more clearly.

items: Passive = be + past participle; agent with *by* only if useful.
*It is said that… / X is said to…*; past: *is said to have done*.
Passive infinitive and -ing forms after verbs and prepositions.
Causative *have/get something done*; *get* is more informal.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Present perfect and aspect: simple, continuous and perfect forms
summary: Tense tells you when; aspect tells you how the speaker sees an action: complete, in progress, or connected to a later moment. Mastering aspect is what makes advanced English sound precise.

blocks.text: English verbs combine **tense** (present or past) with **aspect**. Aspect shows how the speaker views the action:

items: **Simple**: the action is seen as a complete whole or a fact.
**Continuous** (*be* + *-ing*): the action is seen as in progress, temporary or unfinished.
**Perfect** (*have* + past participle): the action is seen from a later point and connected to it.

items.en: I **read** the report.
I **was reading** the report when you called.
items.note: Continuous: in progress at that moment.

items.en: I**'ve read** the report, so I can comment.
I**'ve been reading** reports all morning.
items.note: Perfect continuous: activity up to now, focus on duration.

blocks.text: Present perfect = **have/has + past participle**. Present perfect continuous = **have/has been + -ing**. The auxiliary *have* does all the grammatical work: it carries negation, questions and short answers.
Affirmative
Negative
Questions
Short answers
Short answers repeat only the auxiliary: ~~Yes, I have seen~~ → *Yes, I have.*

blocks.title: The whole perfect family at a glance

head: Form
Structure
Example
rows: I **had been waiting** for an hour.

blocks.title: Spelling of past participles and -ing forms

items: Regular verbs add *-ed*: *work → worked*, *study → studied*, *stop → stopped*.
Irregular participles must be learned: *go → gone*, *write → written*, *take → taken*, *be → been*.
*-ing*: drop silent *-e* (*make → making*), double a final consonant after a short stressed vowel (*run → running*, *begin → beginning*).

sections.title: Main rules: present perfect simple vs past simple

blocks.text: Use the **present perfect** when the past action is connected to now and no finished time is given:

items: experience in an unfinished period: *I've visited Kazan twice.*
a recent change with a present result: *The price has gone up.*
states up to now with *for/since*: *We've known each other since school.*

blocks.text: Use the **past simple** with a finished time or when the story is clearly in the past:

items.en: I **lived** in Berlin in 2019.
~~I have lived in Berlin in 2019.~~
items.note: A finished time expression needs the past simple.

items.en: **Have you seen** the new exhibition? ~ Yes, I **went** last week.
items.note: The conversation starts in the present perfect, then moves to past simple for details.

blocks.text: Expressions that mean "up to now" go with the present perfect. Expressions that point to a **finished** time go with the past simple.

head: Present perfect
Past simple
rows: **this week / today / this year** (period not finished)

blocks.text: Where the adverbs go

items.en: I've **just** sent it.
items.note: *just, already, ever, never* go between *have* and the participle.

items.en: Have you finished **yet**? / I haven't finished **yet**.
items.note: *yet* goes at the end in questions and negatives.

items.en: She's **already** left. / Has she left **already**?
items.note: *already* at the end of a question shows surprise.

items.en: We've lived here **for** ten years / **since** 2015.

items: *for* + length of time: *for a week*, *for ages*.
*since* + point in time: *since Monday*, *since I moved*.
*ago* = back from now, past simple only: *a week ago* (~~I've arrived a week ago~~).

blocks.text: *How long* + present perfect asks about duration up to now; *When* asks about a finished moment and needs the past simple: ~~When have you arrived?~~ → *When did you arrive?*

sections.title: Simple or continuous? Results versus activity

blocks.text: The **simple** form focuses on the result or quantity; the **continuous** form focuses on the activity, its duration, or the fact that it may be unfinished.

items.en: I**'ve painted** the kitchen.
items.note: Finished: the result is a painted kitchen.

items.en: I**'ve been painting** the kitchen.
items.note: Activity: maybe unfinished; explains paint on my clothes.

items.en: She**'s written** 2,000 words today.
~~She's been writing 2,000 words today.~~
items.note: Don't use continuous with a completed number.

blocks.text: **State verbs** (*know, believe, own, belong, seem, consist*) are normally not used in the continuous: *I've known her for years*, not ~~I've been knowing~~.

items: **Repeated actions**: *He's been calling me all week* (irritation, repetition).
**Temporary situations**: *I'm living with my parents at the moment* versus *I live in Riga* (permanent).
**Dynamic uses of state verbs** change meaning: *I'm thinking about it* (considering) / *I think so* (opinion); *She's having lunch* (eating) / *She has a car* (owns).
**This is the first time…** requires the present perfect: *This is the first time I've flown business class.*

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: *How long have you been learning English?*
asks about duration up to now
she is there now or on her way
*I've been working here for two years.*
almost the same; continuous stresses the ongoing activity

items.en: ~~I am living here since 2018.~~
items.note: Russian uses the present tense here; English needs the present perfect: *I've lived / I've been living here since 2018.*

items.en: ~~When have you arrived?~~
items.note: Questions with *when* point to a finished time: *When did you arrive?*

items.en: ~~I've been knowing him for years.~~
items.note: State verb: *I've known him for years.*

items.en: ~~Since three years I work here.~~
items.note: *since* + point in time, *for* + period: *I've worked here for three years.*

blocks.text: At C1, aspect becomes a **choice that shapes meaning and tone**:

items: The continuous can sound **less direct and more polite**: *I was wondering if you could help* (softer than *I wondered*).
The continuous can show **annoyance**: *You're always interrupting me.*
The present perfect is used in news to **introduce** a story, then the past simple gives details: *A major earthquake has struck the region. It hit at 3 a.m.*
The perfect aspect in non-finite forms: *Having finished the report, she left*; *She seems to have forgotten.*

items.en: I**'ve been meaning** to call you.
items.note: continuous perfect for an intention that hasn't happened yet

blocks.text: Academic writing uses the present perfect to **summarise research up to now** and the past simple for **a specific study**:

items.en: Several studies **have examined** the link between sleep and memory. Walker (2017) **found** that…

blocks.text: In academic prose, the present perfect continuous is rarer; prefer *Research has increasingly focused on…* to ~~Researchers have been looking at…~~.

items: Simple = complete whole or fact; continuous = in progress or temporary; perfect = connected to a later point.
Present perfect for unfinished periods and present relevance; past simple for finished times.
Simple for results and quantities; continuous for activity and duration.
State verbs avoid the continuous unless the meaning changes.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Perfect and passive infinitives and -ing forms: to have done, being done, having been done
summary: Infinitives and -ing forms can show time and voice too. Learn how "to have done", "being asked" and "having been told" add earlier time and passive meaning, and why they make advanced writing precise and compact.

blocks.text: Finite verbs show time and voice through tense and *be* + past participle: *He **was told**. She **has finished**.* But many structures need a **non-finite** form — an infinitive (*to do*) or an *-ing* form (*doing*) — after verbs, adjectives, prepositions and in reporting patterns. These forms can also carry **perfect** meaning (an earlier time) and **passive** meaning (the subject receives the action):

items: *I'd like **to be consulted**.* (passive infinitive)
*She seems **to have left**.* (perfect infinitive)
*He hates **being interrupted**.* (passive -ing)
***Having been warned**, they took precautions.* (perfect passive -ing)

blocks.text: Choose the non-finite form in two steps: **time** (same time → simple; earlier time → perfect) and **voice** (subject does it → active; subject receives it → passive).

sections.title: How it works: time and voice without tense

blocks.text: A non-finite verb has no tense of its own, so its time is understood **relative to the main verb**.

items: A **simple** form shows the same time or a later time: *She seems **to know** the answer* (now). *I hope **to finish** soon* (later).

A **perfect** form (*to have done, having done*) shows an **earlier** time, or completion before a point: *She seems **to have known** the answer all along* (earlier). *I hope **to have finished** by June* (completed before June).
A **passive** form (*to be done, being done*) shows that the subject is affected by the action: *Nobody likes **being criticised** in public.*
The **continuous** infinitive (*to be doing*) shows an action in progress: *He seems **to be working** late again.*

blocks.text: The forms combine, giving eight possibilities, though the perfect passive continuous is very rare.
Negatives place *not* before the non-finite form: *I regret **not having asked**. She pretended **not to have heard**.*
1. After seem, appear, happen, tend, claim, pretend

These verbs are followed by an infinitive whose time is relative to the main verb. Compare *He **seems to be** happy* (now) with *He **seems to have been** happy there* (earlier) and *He **seemed to have forgotten** us* (earlier than a past moment).
2. Passive reporting structures
With *say, believe, think, know, report, expect, consider, estimate*, the pattern **subject + passive reporting verb + to-infinitive** is common in news and academic writing:

items: *The painting **is believed to be** a forgery.* (belief now, about now)
*The fire **is thought to have started** in the kitchen.* (belief now, about the past)
*The company **is reported to be negotiating** a merger.* (in progress)
*Two people **are known to have been injured**.* (past + passive)

blocks.text: 3. After verbs and prepositions that take -ing

After *avoid, deny, admit, remember, regret, resent, risk, mind*, and after any preposition, use *being done* for passive meaning and *having done* to stress an earlier action: *She **denied having taken** the documents. They **complained about being kept** waiting. He **resented not being invited**.* With *deny, admit, regret, remember*, the simple -ing often already implies an earlier time, so *having* is a choice for emphasis: *He admitted **taking** / **having taken** the money.*
4. After adjectives and nouns
*It's a privilege **to have been chosen**. I was lucky **to be offered** the job. There's a risk of **being misunderstood**.*
5. Perfect infinitive after modal-like and unreal expressions

Perfect infinitives express unreal or unfulfilled past events after *would like, would rather, would hate, was/were to, was supposed to, meant to*: *I **would like to have seen** her face* (but I didn't). *They **were to have married** in June* (but the wedding was cancelled).
6. Perfect participle clauses

*Having + past participle* at the start of a sentence shows that one action was completed before another, and is typical of formal narrative and reports: ***Having reviewed** the evidence, the panel recommended no further action.* ***Having been rejected** twice, he finally won the grant.*

items.en: The bridge **is expected to be completed** next spring.
The ship **is thought to have sunk** in a storm in 1847.
items.note: present belief about a past event: perfect infinitive

items.en: She doesn't like **being told** what to do.
I'm sorry **to have kept** you waiting.
**Having lived** abroad for years, she found the return difficult.
The documents appear **to have been altered** after signing.
items.note: perfect passive: earlier, and the documents were affected

items.en: He claims **to be writing** a novel.
items.note: in progress at the time of claiming

items.en: I would rather **not have known**.
items.note: unreal past: I did know, and I wish I hadn't

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *He seems to work hard* vs *He seems to be working hard*
*She is said to live in Rome* vs *She is said to have lived in Rome*
*It is said that…* vs *X is said to…*
same meaning; the personal construction (*X is said to*) puts the topic first and is more compact.
*I remember telling him* vs *I remember being told*
I told him vs someone told me.
both show sequence; *having finished* is more formal and works without a preposition.
*I'd like to see it* vs *I'd like to have seen it*
a present/future wish vs regret about the past.

blocks.text: Passive reporting structures (*is believed to, is estimated to have*) and perfect participle clauses are hallmarks of formal writing: they make claims impersonal and compress two clauses into one. In conversation, people usually say *They think the fire started in the kitchen* or *After I'd read it, I…*.
Avoid stacking several non-finite forms in one sentence (*Having been asked to have been seen…*): this sounds heavy even in academic prose. Use a finite clause instead.

items.en: ~~He is said to be born in Vienna.~~
items.note: He is said **to have been born** in Vienna. (the birth was in the past)

items.en: ~~I hate to be interrupted when I'm working.~~
items.note: I hate **being interrupted** when I'm working. (both possible, but -ing is more natural for a general dislike)

items.en: ~~Having finished the report, the computer crashed.~~
items.note: **When I had** finished the report, the computer crashed. (dangling participle: the computer didn't finish the report)

items.en: ~~She denied to have taken the money.~~
items.note: She denied **taking / having taken** the money.

items.en: ~~The suspect is believed having left the country.~~
items.note: The suspect is believed **to have left** the country.

blocks.text: A perfect participle clause must share the subject of the main clause. ***Having been repaired**, the engineers tested the engine* says that the engineers were repaired. Write: *Once the engine had been repaired, the engineers tested it.*
Hedged reporting in academic writing

Passive reporting with *appear, seem* and perfect infinitives lets writers report evidence cautiously: *The effect **appears to have been overestimated** in earlier studies.* Compare the stronger *Earlier studies overestimated the effect.*
Narrative compression

Literary and journalistic prose uses perfect and passive -ing clauses to move quickly: ***Having been** turned away by three publishers, the manuscript finally appeared in 1952, **to be praised** by critics and **ignored** by readers.* The final infinitive of result (*to be praised*) is a C2 stylistic device: it presents a later, often ironic, outcome.
Was to have + past participle

*was/were to have done* describes a planned event that did **not** happen: *The minister **was to have opened** the hospital, but she fell ill.* Compare *was to open* (planned; outcome unknown or it did happen).

items: Non-finite forms show time relative to the main verb: simple = same or later time, perfect = earlier time.
Passive non-finite forms: *to be done, being done, to have been done, having been done*.
Passive reporting: *X is said / believed / thought to do / to be doing / to have done*.
*Having done* clauses show a completed earlier action and must share the main clause subject.
*Would like / was supposed to / was to* + perfect infinitive = an unfulfilled past plan or wish.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Prepositional phrases: fixed expressions beginning with a preposition
summary: Phrases such as in charge of, by mistake, on behalf of and under pressure work as single units. Knowing them makes your English more precise and idiomatic, especially in formal writing.

blocks.text: A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and works as one block of meaning: *at risk*, *in favour of*, *on purpose*. Many are fixed: you can't change the preposition or add an article.

items.en: The species is **at risk of** extinction.
I deleted the file **by mistake**.
She spoke **on behalf of** the whole team.

head: Structure
Examples
rows: **at** first, **by** chance, **in** time, **on** time, **out of** order
**on the** whole, **in the** end, **at the** moment, **by the** way

blocks.text: Many fixed phrases have **no article**: *at risk, in debt, on foot, by car, under pressure* (~~in a debt~~, ~~by the car~~).
at
*at first, at last, at least, at once, at risk, at random, at a loss (for words), at short notice, at your disposal, at stake*
